title: What a Market Solves
description: A market exists to solve one problem: a buyer and a seller who cannot find each other. Derive the order book, the spread and the market maker from that problem, with no chart.

title: The Order Book
description: The order book is every resting limit order at every price, and the quote is only its top line. Walk a market order through it and watch slippage appear from arithmetic alone.

title: What a Fill Actually Is
description: Your order meets one specific counterparty who chose that moment to trade against you. Why that makes your fills a biased sample, and what it costs.

title: The Spread Is the Price of Immediacy
description: The spread in cents tells you nothing. Divided by your stop it gives the win rate you need just to break even, from one formula: (1 + spread/stop) / 2.

title: Why Anyone Quotes At All
description: A market maker faces two risks: the position they did not want, and the customer who knows more. Both are visible in the spread, and both predict when liquidity disappears.

title: The Candle Is a Summary
description: A candle keeps five numbers and discards everything else that happened. Knowing exactly which five decides which questions it can answer.

title: Time and Sales
description: The tape is the transaction record. It carries three facts, and the fourth one your platform shows you is inferred rather than reported.

title: Volume and Delta
description: Volume counts contracts, and every one of them was bought and sold. Delta counts something else: which side was unwilling to wait.

title: Who Else Is Here
description: Four kinds of participant, sorted by what they want rather than how big they are. The reason someone is in the book predicts what they do.

title: Every Trade Starts Negative
description: Spread, commission, slippage and financing are charged whether the trade works or not. Their sum, divided by what you have at risk, is the bar your edge has to clear.

title: Slippage and Impact at Retail Size
description: What a fill costs is your size divided by the size resting in front of you. Below the touch you pay the spread; above it you buy the walk, and it grows faster than your order does.

title: What Should You Actually Trade
description: Rank instruments by what a round trip costs as a share of what they move in a day. An index ETF gives up 0.2% of its range; a $1.50 micro-cap gives up 37%.

title: What You Are Actually Buying
description: A share, a futures contract, an option and a perpetual are four different legal objects. The object fixes the smallest position you may take, whether it expires, and the most it can take from you.

title: Margin and Leverage
description: Margin is the collateral you post to hold a position, not a measure of what it can lose. If your leverage is 10x, a 10% move against you is the whole deposit.

title: When Your Broker Acts Without You
description: Five published rules let someone else act in your account without asking. The price at which the first of them fires is loan divided by one minus the maintenance requirement, and you can compute it today.

title: Sim Against Live
description: A simulator sets every cost this module measured to zero. A strategy that reports +$1,000 over a hundred trades can net minus $700 once they are put back, and the breakeven win rate moves from 50% to 58.5%.

title: Expectancy
description: An edge is a number: E = p times b minus (1 minus p), measured in units of what you risk. At a reward-to-risk of 0.25 you need to be right 80% of the time; at 5 you need 16.7%.

title: What an Edge Feels Like
description: At a 45% win rate, eight losses in a row turns up in more than half of all 200-trade samples and arrives on average every 263 trades. Streak length depends on your win rate alone. The drawdown that threatens the account is a different and larger number.

title: How Long Until You Know
description: Expectancy is a measurement, and its error bar is wider than the number inside it. A halved edge takes around 571 trades to establish, and putting your costs back takes the sample from 143 trades to 540.

title: Position Sizing
description: Position size = (account times the fraction you risk) divided by the distance to your stop. The fraction is chosen from the drawdown you can keep trading through, not the return you want: at 3% a trade a one-in-twenty bad run costs 39% and needs 65% to undo.

title: Where the Stop Goes
description: A stop belongs beyond the price that would prove the trade wrong, not at a percentage of your account, because the market has never seen your account. The level says where the reason dies; ATR says how much room ordinary movement needs.

title: Risk of Ruin
description: Ruin is computable from three numbers you already have: your edge, the fraction you risk and how far you are allowed to fall. It is not driven by bad luck. At 1% of a winning system not one run in two hundred thousand halved; at 10% of the same system, sixteen in a hundred did.

title: Keeping the Record
description: Ten fields, written down at the time, decide whether any question in this module can be answered about your own trading. Two of them cannot be recovered afterwards at any price, and a broker statement contains neither.

title: When the Drawdown Arrives
description: This module priced the drawdown you are in. It has not priced what you are about to do about it, and that is the larger number: at 5% a trade, sizing up returns you to the high in nine careers out of ten and digs the hole to twice its depth in nearly half of them.

title: Where Liquidity Rests
description: Stop orders are market orders that have not happened yet, and they collect at a handful of prices because the rules for placing them are few and shared. That clustering explains the shape of a level being broken and rejoined, and it decides how far beyond the level your own stop has to sit.

title: The Order Book Is Theater
description: A resting order costs nothing to place and nothing to withdraw, so the size on the screen is a statement of intent rather than a commitment. What that leaves you with is a guess about intent, and the value of that guess turns out to depend almost entirely on a number about the instrument rather than a skill of yours.

title: The Liquidity Lie
description: Deliberate manipulation of a market is real, is prosecuted, and looks almost nothing like the version you were told. The proved conduct runs at institutional size against other machines, for a tick or two, and the story that it is aimed at your stop is not merely unsupported -- it has a price, and lesson 25 already computed it.

title: Absorption and Exhaustion
description: When price finally reaches a level, one thing becomes a fact: volume was spent there and the level held or it did not. Everything a footprint adds on top of that is a classification with a known error rate, and the same footprint supports two opposite stories in the folklore -- which is the finding, not a complaint.

title: Volume at Price
description: A session’s volume is not spread evenly over the prices it visited, and unlike a delta the count itself needs no inference at all. The single number everyone quotes from it does: the point of control is the tallest bar of a histogram, and on one session it moves across 63% of the range depending on a bin width nobody chose deliberately.

title: Volume Profile
description: A value area asks a better question than a point of control and is about three times steadier under the same binning. It is still not what it says on the tin: the box labelled 70% holds anywhere from 70% to 84% of the day depending on a setting, and widening the window from one session to two puts half of the heavier day’s value area outside value entirely.

title: Hidden Size
description: Showing size costs money, so the people who have it do not show it, and the screen understates as routinely as it overstates. Detecting a reserve is an observation rather than a read — and in the record below the detector could not have fired at all on eighty tests in a hundred, which is why a quiet book proves nothing.

title: Market Structure
description: A break of structure and a change of character are the only two chart claims that predict something countable, which makes them worth more than every pattern with a name. What nobody quotes is the swing definition they were computed from. On the twenty bars below the same prices give eight structure events, or two, or none.

title: Order Blocks and Displacement
description: An order block is the last opposite-coloured candle before a strong move away from it. That sentence contains three settings and no observations. On the twenty bars of lesson 32, now with bodies, ordinary choices give ten order blocks, or five, or four, or two.

title: Divergence
description: A divergence is price disagreeing with a number computed from price. Two settings decide whether one exists: a swing rule and an oscillator period. On the sixty closes below, ordinary values give three divergences, or two, or one, or none.

title: Sweeps, Beyond the First
description: A sweep is price trading past a level and coming back. Three settings decide whether one happened: which levels count, whether a wick past is enough, and how soon back inside still counts. On the sixty bars below, ordinary settings find five sweeps, or fifteen, or forty-six.

title: Markets Have Modes
description: The crudest regime measurement is one ratio: how much of the distance price travelled ended up as progress. On the sixty closes below it separates the two stretches cleanly. Change the window from ten closes to thirty and the two readings disagree on twenty-two of thirty bars.

title: Detecting a Regime Change
description: Finding where a finished series changed and deciding that it has just changed are two different problems. On the sixty closes below, one bar of confirmation halves the declared changes from eight to four and five bars halves it again — and how much of the move you are inside goes seven, four, three, two, then ten out of ten.

title: What a Timeframe Is
description: A bar is not something the market produced. It is a rule for grouping the tape, with two settings, and only one of them ever gets quoted. Regroup the sixty bars of the last four lessons and the high and the low do not move at all while the swing count falls from fifteen to one.

title: Trading More Than One
description: Three charts of one instrument are three readings of one tape. On the sixty bars of the last six lessons they agree on nine bars in forty, and requiring all three to call a trend leaves seven. What the filtering is worth is arithmetic, and it has two break-even points, not one.

title: Multi-Day Structure
description: Every rule of the last eight lessons was built on a series with no holes in it. Take the same sixty closes and remove the overlap between bars: nineteen of thirty-nine transitions become gaps, the high and the low do not move, and a stop resting inside a gap fills at a median of one and a half times its intended loss.

title: The Session Cycle
description: A session is the interval between two closures, and its edges concentrate activity for three structural reasons that have nothing to do with mood. But split this module’s sixty bars into three consecutive twenties and the efficiency ratio reads 0.021, 0.067 and 0.333 on a series with no clock in it at all.
